S01.why: He is competing (insists, refuses to discuss). The issue matters and the relationship continues, and the tool is internal, so there is time: collaborate on a scoped fix that fits his release plan, with the risk and an owner written down.

S02.why: Ignoring emails and skipping meetings is avoiding. A certificate that expires in two days is urgent and high-stakes: be assertive, go to the accountable owner (RACI), and get it renewed now; repair the relationship afterwards.

S03.why: A joint workshop exploring options that meet both teams' goals is classic collaborating, and it is the right choice for a high-stakes topic with time available.

S04.why: Splitting the work is compromising. After a polarised debate (stage 2), a time-boxed compromise on a low-stakes, urgent item keeps work moving; check the order is risk-based (internet-facing servers first).

S05.why: Giving in to keep the peace is accommodating. Input validation is a high-stakes control, so accommodating is the wrong mode: bring the abuse case and ASVS requirement, and agree a minimal version together.

S06.why: Insisting and recruiting allies is competing; coalitions and taking sides is Glasl stage 4 (win-lose). Bring in a neutral facilitator and move to collaborating on a design decision record: the answer is usually both (gateway coarse checks, app object checks).

S07.why: A fait accompli ('my way') is competing and Glasl stage 3 (actions, not words). A disabled WAF rule on a production integration is urgent and high-stakes: re-enable or replace the control now through the change process, then run a blameless review.

S08.why: An ultimatum ('or else') is Glasl stage 6, strategies of threat. Do not sign under pressure: assertively route the exception to the accountable risk owner with the facts; at stage 6 a manager or mediator should step in.

S09.why: Public blame is Glasl stage 5 (loss of face); staying silent and changing the subject is avoiding. Ask for a private conversation, use a DESC script, and propose a blameless review of the outage.

S10.why: Going along on a low-stakes design choice is accommodating, and that is fine: it builds goodwill you can use when a high-stakes issue comes.

S11.why: Pairing and co-designing around a shared goal is collaborating; with high stakes (secrets in logs) and time available, keep collaborating.

S12.why: Meeting in the middle is compromising; talking past each other is stage 2. For a lower-stakes commercial term under time pressure a compromise is fine, as long as critical-issue fix times are not traded away.
